item.title: Right Ventricular Function from Ammonia PET Predicts Major Cardiac Events in Ischemia - Bioengineer.org
item.description:
요약

  • A clinical study evaluating right ventricular mechanics through nitrogen-13 ammonia positron emission tomography has established that right ventricular fractional area change independently predicts major adverse cardiac events in patients diagnosed with ischemic heart disease.
  • Historically, noninvasive estimation of right ventricular performance has predominantly relied upon transthoracic echocardiography through standard indices such as tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion and fractional area change.
  • The retrospective single-centre investigation reviewed consecutive patients presenting with known or suspected ischemic heart disease between January 2015 and January 2021 who were scheduled for myocardial perfusion imaging.

본문

A clinical study evaluating right ventricular mechanics through nitrogen-13 ammonia positron emission tomography has established that right ventricular fractional area change independently predicts major adverse cardiac events in patients diagnosed with ischemic heart disease. Historically, noninvasive estimation of right ventricular performance has predominantly relied upon transthoracic echocardiography through standard indices such as tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion and fractional area change. However, echocardiographic visualization often faces technical barriers, including suboptimal acoustic windows, irregular right ventricular geometry, and notable observer variability. By applying specialized image-processing methods to cardiac positron emission tomography datasets, researchers sought to establish whether nitrogen-13 ammonia scans could simultaneously quantify right ventricular function and deliver meaningful prognostic risk stratification beyond conventional clinical and imaging parameters.

The retrospective single-centre investigation reviewed consecutive patients presenting with known or suspected ischemic heart disease between January 2015 and January 2021 who were scheduled for myocardial perfusion imaging. Individuals who exhibited adenosine ineffectiveness, had congenital heart malformations, or presented with image artifacts that precluded quantitative analysis were excluded from the primary assessments. In total, the study evaluated two primary cohorts to validate the analytical algorithms and verify long-term prognostic utility. A dedicated comparative group of twenty-eight individuals who underwent both transthoracic echocardiography and nitrogen-13 ammonia positron emission tomography within close proximity provided the foundation for assessing numerical correlation between modalities. To determine optimal prognostic cutoffs and validate event prediction, three hundred and fifty patients were assigned to a primary investigation cohort and an independent validation cohort using a four-to-three random distribution, with the main clinical cohort comprising two hundred patients tracked over a mean follow-up duration of forty plus or minus twenty-three months.

item.title: Scientists find way to repair heart damage after a heart attack - 1News
item.description:
요약

  • Every year, millions of people worldwide suffer a heart attack.
  • Yet surviving a heart attack is not necessarily the end of the story.
  • Although this is still early-stage research, the study offers the tantalising possibility that one day we might be able to encourage the adult human heart to regenerate damaged muscle.

본문

Every year, millions of people worldwide suffer a heart attack. Thanks to advances in emergency treatment, many now survive an event that might once have been fatal. Yet surviving a heart attack is not necessarily the end of the story. The damage can be permanent, increasing the risk of heart failure, breathlessness and a poorer quality of life.

By David C. Gaze for The Conversation

Researchers have developed an experimental treatment that could change how we approach recovery after a heart attack. Rather than simply protecting the remaining heart muscle, the new approach aims to encourage the heart to repair itself. So far, it has only been tested in mice.

The findings, published in the journal Nature Cardiovascular Research, describe how modified messenger RNA (mRNA) can encourage heart muscle cells to multiply, potentially improving the heart’s ability to pump blood.

Although this is still early-stage research, the study offers the tantalising possibility that one day we might be able to encourage the adult human heart to regenerate damaged muscle.

Why the heart struggles to repair itself

A heart attack (myocardial infarction) occurs when blood flow through a coronary artery is significantly reduced or even fully blocked. Without oxygen, the cells of the heart muscle begin to die. These specialised cells, called cardiomyocytes, are responsible for the continuous contractions of the heart muscle, which pumps blood around the body to our vital organs.

Unlike skin or liver tissue, the adult human heart has limited capacity to replace damaged cells. Instead, dead muscle is largely replaced by fibrous scar tissue. Although this scar helps maintain the heart’s structural integrity, it cannot contract like healthy muscle.

The consequence is a heart that may become progressively weaker, sometimes leading to heart failure.

Modern treatments, such as procedures to reopen blocked arteries, medication and supervised exercise programmes, have greatly improved survival. But they cannot replace heart muscle that has already died.

During the early development of the heart, the cardiomyocytes divide, allowing the heart muscle to grow. Shortly after birth, most mammalian cardiomyocytes largely lose this ability. The researchers investigated whether they could restart this process by making heart muscle cells produce two proteins, called Myc and cyclin T1.

Myc switches on genes involved in cell growth and division, while cyclin T1 helps activate the machinery cells need to multiply. Together, the proteins can encourage mature heart muscle cells to start dividing again.

The researchers used modified mRNA to give heart muscle cells instructions for making the two proteins. This is the same basic technology used in COVID vaccines, which deliver temporary genetic instructions to cells to make a protein that trains the immune system to recognise the virus.

item.title: Resistance Training to Failure Boosts Strength in Frail Older Adults Across Intensities - Bioengineer.org
item.description:
요약

  • Frailty represents a widespread geriatric syndrome defined by progressive physiological deterioration across multiple bodily systems, causing notable declines in muscular capacity, physical mobility, and functional autonomy.
  • Traditional physical exercise guidelines, including recommendations from the American College of Sports Medicine, have historically asserted that heavy loading reaching or exceeding eighty percent of one-repetition maximum is necessary to maximize strength adaptations.
  • Across the final evaluable cohort of 234 participants, progressive resistance training executed to volitional muscular failure produced substantial, statistically significant gains in maximal lower-body strength regardless of assigned intensity.

본문

Frailty represents a widespread geriatric syndrome defined by progressive physiological deterioration across multiple bodily systems, causing notable declines in muscular capacity, physical mobility, and functional autonomy. Traditional physical exercise guidelines, including recommendations from the American College of Sports Medicine, have historically asserted that heavy loading reaching or exceeding eighty percent of one-repetition maximum is necessary to maximize strength adaptations. While heavier resistance challenges neuromuscular pathways and prompts earlier recruitment of higher-threshold motor units in healthy adults, frail community-dwelling older individuals frequently encounter structural, medical, and psychological barriers to high-intensity loading. Moreover, medical practitioners and geriatric care professionals frequently hesitate to prescribe strenuous high-intensity strength programs to vulnerable seniors due to safety concerns and compliance difficulties. However, evidence derived from exercise physiology indicates that executing resistance exercise sets to volitional muscular failure stimulates progressive motor unit recruitment as underlying muscle fibers fatigue, suggesting that lower mechanical loads might elicit comparable physiological adaptations.

To evaluate whether an optimal loading threshold exists for frail older populations, investigators conducted the TEAMS study, a twelve-week, two-step randomized controlled trial based in the Amsterdam Metropolitan Area. Conducted under rigorous clinical standards in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and registered under trial identifier NL-OMON54919, the trial recruited community-dwelling older adults aged sixty-five and older between September 2020 and September 2023. Screened volunteers were medically evaluated by a study physician to exclude candidates presenting unstable coronary heart disease, severe heart failure exceeding New York Heart Association functional class three, severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, active systemic oncological therapies, or neurodegenerative conditions. The enrolled cohort demonstrated substantial clinical complexity, with eighty-nine percent reporting two or more chronic health conditions, thirty percent managing polypharmacy involving five or more daily medications, and an overall mean participant age of seventy-four years.

item.title: ‘The Challenge’ Star Tyler Duckworth’s Cause of Death at 44 Revealed - Us Weekly
item.description:
요약

  • The Challenge star Tyler Duckworth’s cause of death has been revealed.
  • The North Dakota State Forensic Examiner’s Office confirmed to Us on Friday, November 27, that Tyler died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease.
  • In the wake of Tyler’s death, many of his former costars — who turned into dear friends — have honored the reality star who left a former mark on The Challenge franchise.

본문

The Challenge star Tyler Duckworth’s cause of death has been revealed.

The North Dakota State Forensic Examiner’s Office confirmed to Us on Friday, November 27, that Tyler died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease. His manner of death was ruled natural.

The Cleveland Clinic states that hypertensive heart disease can cause problems because of long-term, unmanaged high blood pressure. The added strain on one’s heart can lead to heart failure. (TMZ was first to report the news.)

News broke on August 13 that Tyler had died at the age of 44.

“My son, Tyler, passed away earlier this week,” Tyler’s mom, Jodi Duckworth, wrote via Facebook at the time. “Cause of death has yet to be determined. I will post on Facebook about services as soon as his dad and I figure it out.”

The Grand Forks Police Department later confirmed to Us that its officers had responded to a welfare check on August 11. When they arrived, Tyler was found unresponsive and determined to be deceased.

Tyler’s death came nearly two weeks after he appeared at The Challenge Mania event in Minneapolis. In his final social media post before his death, the reality star expressed how excited he was to interact with fans and meet with fellow competitors, including Paulie Calafiore, Mark Long and Rachel Robinson.

“So proud to represent my hometown of Minneapolis along with these other Challenge legends,” Tyler wrote via Instagram on August 2. “The fans are what keep us coming out! Hearing your stories of courage, inspiration & joy that you’ve got being a fan of the franchise is humbling each and every time.”

Fans met Tyler when he appeared on MTV’s The Real World: Key West in 2006 shortly after graduating from Tufts University.

He went on to compete on six seasons of The Challenge, including The Duel, The Gauntlet III, Cutthroat, Rivals, All Stars 2 and All Stars 3. He was crowned the champion on both Cutthroat and Rivals.

“The Challenge community is gutted to hear of Tyler Duckworth’s remarkably untimely passing. The young man who first came into our universe as a comical and sensitive personality developed into a force who would become a two-time champion, and he will be sorely missed,” showrunner Justin Booth said in a statement to Variety. “We are devastated, and we send our most heartfelt condolences to his family and friends. Rest in peace, young man.”

In the wake of Tyler’s death, many of his former costars — who turned into dear friends — have honored the reality star who left a former mark on The Challenge franchise.

“We shared something special being part of The Challenge family,” veteran and champion Brad Fiorenza wrote via Instagram on August 13. “I’ll always be grateful for the memories we shared. … Tyler will be deeply missed by so many. May his amazing soul live on in the lives he’s touched. RIP my dear friend 🕊️🙏.”

item.title: Scientists Track Heart Health for 34 Years—Find Risk Decades Before Event - Newsweek
item.description:
요약

  • Patients will often speak about symptoms they experienced moments before a stroke or heart attack, but new research suggests warning signs may emerge as much as 30 years before the event.
  • A research team led by the University of Edinburgh in Scotland examined data from more than 100,000 people between 1985 and 2019, looking at how multiple cardiovascular risk factors changed over time.
  • The researchers found that several cardiovascular risk factors began following different patterns in people who later experienced a heart attack, stroke or another cardiovascular event.

본문

Patients will often speak about symptoms they experienced moments before a stroke or heart attack, but new research suggests warning signs may emerge as much as 30 years before the event.

A research team led by the University of Edinburgh in Scotland examined data from more than 100,000 people between 1985 and 2019, looking at how multiple cardiovascular risk factors changed over time.

Dr. Mike MacDonald, a leading consultant cardiologist who was not involved in the study, told Newsweek: “This study confirms that in most people heart attacks and strokes rarely come out of the blue.”

Read More on Life

In the United States, one person dies every 34 seconds from cardiovascular disease, according to the CDC. While stroke risk increases with age, strokes can occur at any age. In 2022, one in six deaths from cardiovascular disease in the U.S., or 17.5 percent, was due to stroke.

Warning Signs May Emerge Decades Earlier

The researchers found that several cardiovascular risk factors began following different patterns in people who later experienced a heart attack, stroke or another cardiovascular event.

These included established risk factors such as high blood pressure and diabetes, as well as measures of kidney function.

Differences were also detected in blood biomarkers more than a decade before some participants went on to experience a cardiovascular event.

The findings suggest there may be a significant window in which identifying and addressing risk factors could help reduce the likelihood of serious cardiovascular disease later in life.

Dr. Dorien Kimenai, British Heart Foundation Research Fellow at the Usher Institute at the University of Edinburgh, told Newsweek: “Our study clearly illustrates that modifiable risk factor patterns diverge long before a heart attack or stroke occurs. Prevention is key. Regular cardiovascular health checks from the age of 40 are important and can ultimately help reduce the number of heart attacks and strokes.

What Are the Risk Factors?

Traditional risk factors, including high blood pressure and cholesterol, have long been associated with cardiovascular disease. However, previous research has often examined individual risk factors rather than tracking how several of them change over long periods of time.

MacDonald told Newsweek: “The problem is that most risk calculating tools that doctors use look ten years ahead, so people in their 30s and 40s are labelled low risk and these initial signals are ignored.

“This is observational data and doses not prove causation, however, the message is clear: know your numbers early and act on them.”

He emphasizes that it is easier to prevent a heart attack and stroke than many people may think, but action needs to begin 20 to 30 years beforehand.

Other measures, including kidney function and biomarkers found in the blood, may also help build a broader picture of a person's cardiovascular risk.

item.title: Study reveals biological trade-off between heartbeat and cardiac regeneration - News-Medical
item.description:
요약

  • The human heart beats more than 100,000 times a day, tirelessly pumping blood to deliver oxygen and nutrients throughout the body.
  • Yet despite its remarkable endurance, the heart has a major limitation: it has almost no capacity to repair itself after injury.
  • To maintain the continuous contractions required to sustain life, heart muscle cells, known as cardiomyocytes, sacrifice much of their ability to divide and regenerate.

본문

The human heart beats more than 100,000 times a day, tirelessly pumping blood to deliver oxygen and nutrients throughout the body. Yet despite its remarkable endurance, the heart has a major limitation: it has almost no capacity to repair itself after injury. A new study, co-funded by the ERC, led by researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) helps explain why.

The research reveals a fundamental biological trade-off at the core of heart function. To maintain the continuous contractions required to sustain life, heart muscle cells, known as cardiomyocytes, sacrifice much of their ability to divide and regenerate.

Published today in Nature Cardiovascular Research, the study demonstrates that the mechanical activity of cardiomyocytes acts as a barrier to regeneration. The findings identify a previously unknown connection between contraction, energy metabolism, and cell division, providing new insight into one of the greatest challenges in cardiovascular medicine.

The heart has evolved to prioritize continuous function over regeneration. Our findings show that cardiomyocytes face a fundamental biological trade-off: the very machinery that enables them to contract and sustain life also prevents them from dividing and replacing damaged tissue."

Dr. Florian Weinberger, group leader of the Cardiac Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Therapies Laboratory at CNIC and senior author of the study

Unlike tissues such as the skin or liver, which can readily replace damaged cells, the adult heart has very limited regenerative capacity. This ability is rapidly lost shortly after birth, precisely when the heart begins to experience increased workload as it adapts to life outside the womb.

To investigate whether the heart's constant mechanical activity contributes to this loss of regeneration, the CNIC team examined cardiomyocytes across multiple experimental systems, including human stem cell-derived heart cells, engineered heart tissue, living myocardial slices, and animal models.

The researchers found that when cardiomyocyte contraction was temporarily inhibited, the cells underwent dramatic changes. Their highly organized contractile structures, known as sarcomeres, became disassembled, and the cells re-entered the cell cycle, showing a significantly increased capacity to divide.

Remarkably, when contraction was restored, the process reversed. The sarcomeres reassembled, and the cells once again exited the cell cycle, losing their ability to proliferate.

Further analyses revealed that these structural changes were accompanied by a profound shift in cellular metabolism.

When cardiomyocytes stopped contracting, they adopted a more glycolytic metabolic state, relying less on the energy-demanding processes needed to sustain continuous contraction. This metabolic reprogramming appeared to create conditions that allowed the cells to re-enter the cell cycle and divide.

item.title: Study finds 4 factors preceded 99% of cardiovascular events — ScienceAlert - UA.NEWS
item.description:
요약

  • Study finds 4 factors preceded 99% of cardiovascular events — ScienceAlert
  • As ScienceAlert reports, a 2025 study involving 9 million people in the United States and South Korea found that 99% of cardiovascular events were preceded by at least one of four risk factors.
  • A separate meta-analysis of 51 clinical trials involving more than 350,000 people found that reducing systolic blood pressure by every 5 mmHg was associated with an approximately 12% lower risk of stroke, ischemic heart disease or heart failure during the first year of treatment.

본문

Study finds 4 factors preceded 99% of cardiovascular events — ScienceAlert

As ScienceAlert reports, a 2025 study involving 9 million people in the United States and South Korea found that 99% of cardiovascular events were preceded by at least one of four risk factors. These were above-optimal blood pressure, cholesterol or blood glucose levels, as well as tobacco smoking.

Above-optimal blood pressure was recorded most often before heart attacks, strokes and cases of heart failure: it was present in 93% of such cases. The study of factors preceding cardiovascular events was published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology.

Blood pressure control

A separate meta-analysis of 51 clinical trials involving more than 350,000 people found that reducing systolic blood pressure by every 5 mmHg was associated with an approximately 12% lower risk of stroke, ischemic heart disease or heart failure during the first year of treatment.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

This pattern was similar across five main classes of hypertension drugs: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics. The meta-analysis authors noted that the cardiovascular benefits of antihypertensive therapy emerge early and persist over time.

Other preventive approaches

The article also cites the results of a randomized study in Australia involving nearly 10,000 older people. Over approximately six years, participants taking statins experienced cardiovascular events 30% less often.

Large randomized trials also link drugs in the GLP-1 agonist class, including semaglutide, to a reduction in major cardiovascular events. In an analysis of data from one trial, patients with type 2 diabetes and a history of heart failure who took daily semaglutide were 22% less likely to require hospitalization or emergency care for heart failure or to die from cardiovascular causes than the placebo group. No such effect was recorded for participants without a history of heart failure.

item.title: Major Study Links 99% of Heart Attacks And Strokes With Just 4 Risk Factors - ScienceAlert
item.description:
요약

  • The onset of a heart attack or stroke can take many by surprise – but most cases do not appear out of nowhere.
  • In a 2025 study of 9 million people from the US and South Korea, 99 percent of all cardiovascular events were preceded by either above-optimal blood pressure, cholesterol, or blood sugar levels, or tobacco smoking.
  • More studies are needed to confirm how drugs for blood glucose, hypertension, and cholesterol might work to protect the heart, but evidence increasingly suggests that they are doing something positive.

본문

The onset of a heart attack or stroke can take many by surprise – but most cases do not appear out of nowhere.

Nearly everyone who suffers a major cardiovascular event has at least one of four risk factors in the lead-up, according to recent research.

In a 2025 study of 9 million people from the US and South Korea, 99 percent of all cardiovascular events were preceded by either above-optimal blood pressure, cholesterol, or blood sugar levels, or tobacco smoking.

Raised blood pressure was the leading culprit.

It was present before 93 percent of heart attacks, strokes, or heart failure events.

The findings suggest that staying on top of certain health risks, like blood pressure, can help patients avoid serious, potentially fatal outcomes later in life.

This year, we got more evidence of just that.

A new meta-analysis of 51 trials has shown that treating hypertension can lead to rapid and lasting cardiovascular benefits.

The video below has a summary:

Across more than 350,000 participants, every 5 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure was associated with a roughly 12 percent lower risk of stroke, ischemic heart disease, or heart failure during the first year of treatment.

What's more, this pattern was broadly consistent across five major classes of blood pressure drugs: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and diuretics.

All of these medications seemed to help.

"Our findings show that antihypertensive therapy provides substantial cardiovascular benefits early, which are maintained over time without progressive amplification," the authors of the meta-analysis conclude.

"These findings have potentially major implications for cardiovascular prevention and clinical decision-making."

Historically, many heart attacks are blamed on clogged arteries, but the reality is more complicated, especially for younger people and women.

Recent evidence, for example, has found that more than half of heart attacks in women aged 65 or younger are triggered by causes other than clogged arteries.

If doctors and patients had a clearer idea of which health factors to monitor, some risks to the heart might be managed, potentially preventing future cardiovascular events.

Decades of randomized trials show, for instance, that cholesterol-lowering medications, like statins, can significantly reduce the relative risk of a future cardiovascular event.

According to a 2022 analysis, genetic studies suggest that for every single mmol/l decrease in 'bad cholesterol' levels sustained over a lifetime, the risk of cardiovascular disease drops by more than 50 percent.

What's more, a recent randomized trial from Australia, including nearly 10,000 older adults, found that after roughly six years, those taking statins were 30 percent less likely to suffer a cardiovascular event.

Treating hypertension and cholesterol levels seems to improve cardiovascular outcomes, but improving blood glucose control also shows promise as a potential preventive target.

item.title: Balloon-Assisted Septal Traversal Enables Transcatheter Closure of Acquired Gerbode Defect - Bioengineer.org
item.description:
요약

  • Interventional cardiologists successfully performed a transcatheter closure of an acquired Gerbode defect in a 78-year-old woman by employing a balloon-assisted septal traversal technique while maintaining an arteriovenous loop.
  • The patient had developed heart failure resulting from an abnormal intracardiac shunt communicating between the left ventricular outflow tract and the right atrium.
  • Article Title: Balloon-Assisted Septal Traversal While Maintaining the Arteriovenous Loop to Facilitate Gerbode Defect Closure

본문

Interventional cardiologists successfully performed a transcatheter closure of an acquired Gerbode defect in a 78-year-old woman by employing a balloon-assisted septal traversal technique while maintaining an arteriovenous loop. The patient had developed heart failure resulting from an abnormal intracardiac shunt communicating between the left ventricular outflow tract and the right atrium. This rare anatomical defect emerged after a redo surgical aortic valve replacement to explant a small Trifecta bioprosthetic valve that was unsuitable for a transcatheter valve-in-valve procedure.

Due to the patient’s history of multiple prior sternotomies and an elevated risk profile for additional open-heart surgery, the clinical team pursued a minimally invasive transcatheter repair. The intervention began by establishing an arteriovenous loop connecting the femoral artery to the right internal jugular vein. Operators crossed the septal communication from the left ventricular side using a JR4 diagnostic catheter and a 260-centimeter Terumo Glidewire under combined fluoroscopic visualization and transesophageal echocardiography confirmation, subsequently snaring the wire from within the right internal jugular vein.

Technical complications arose when advancing an 8 French Trevisio delivery sheath from the right internal jugular vein over the established circuit. Because the acquired Gerbode defect occupied a basal anatomical position in close proximity to the aortic valve, the delivery sheath repeatedly prolapsed back into the right atrium whenever operators attempted to remove the arteriovenous loop wire. Furthermore, standard maneuvers to advance the sheath deeper into the left ventricle carried a significant risk of inadvertently crossing or damaging the adjacent aortic valve structure.

To overcome this anatomical limitation, the interventional team re-established the arteriovenous loop and navigated an MP4 catheter through the Trevisio sheath toward the left ventricular apex. The catheter was then exchanged for a dedicated Amplatz wire to provide structural support. Rather than relying on a standard dilator, operators positioned a 6-millimeter Mustang balloon at the tip of the sheath and inflated it to 10 atmospheres, creating a tapered leading edge that allowed smooth passage into the left ventricle while keeping the arteriovenous loop securely intact.

Once stable coaxial access to the left ventricular apex was secured, the inflated balloon and arteriovenous loop were withdrawn. The team selected a 12-millimeter Amplatzer ventricular septal defect occluder to seal the defect, which measured 10 millimeters on transesophageal echocardiography. This sizing adhered to the conventional practice of oversizing the device by 2 to 4 millimeters, with operators opting for a conservative 2-millimeter oversize specifically to minimize mechanical crowding and interference with the adjacent aortic and tricuspid valves.

item.title: Heart Attacks Trigger Brain Inflammation and Autonomic Dysregulation Across the Neurocardiac Axis - Bioengineer.org
item.description:
요약

  • Myocardial infarction triggers a cascade of inflammatory signaling across the neurocardiac axis that contributes to both cardiac and neurocognitive dysfunctions, according to a review published in Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology.
  • The analysis evaluates how cardiogenic trauma disrupts communication between the brain and the heart, initiating pathways of chronic systemic inflammation and compounding damage to both organs.
  • Imbalanced autonomic nervous system synchronization within the neurocardiac axis leads to infarcted or damaged tissues, which may influence potential inflammatory signaling mechanisms in post-infarction pathology and affect acute and chronic outcomes.

본문

Myocardial infarction triggers a cascade of inflammatory signaling across the neurocardiac axis that contributes to both cardiac and neurocognitive dysfunctions, according to a review published in Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology. The analysis evaluates how cardiogenic trauma disrupts communication between the brain and the heart, initiating pathways of chronic systemic inflammation and compounding damage to both organs.

At the center of this pathology is an imbalance in autonomic nervous system synchronization within the neurocardiac network. Normal physiological function depends on undisrupted cardio-regulatory brain regions innervating the heart. Imbalanced autonomic nervous system synchronization within the neurocardiac axis leads to infarcted or damaged tissues, which may influence potential inflammatory signaling mechanisms in post-infarction pathology and affect acute and chronic outcomes.

To assess these complex interactions, authors Cayla Y. Kim, Antoine Sakr, Ryan Bax, Desislava Doycheva, and colleagues synthesized findings from multiple research formats. Their assessment compiles data from in-vitro models alongside in-vivo rodent and porcine experiments involving surgically induced myocardial infarction and heart failure, supplemented by clinical meta-analyses outlining post-infarction pathologies in human populations.

The review details cellular-level responses, focusing specifically on inflammatory cells such as microglia and astrocytes alongside the blood-brain barrier. Following cardiogenic trauma, an exacerbated stress response and persistent systemic inflammation progressively weaken the blood-brain barrier. This breakdown prolongs neuroinflammation and damages vital neurological sites responsible for cardiac regulation and tissue repair.

Beyond direct cellular pathways, the researchers reviewed supplemental perspectives addressing broader systemic contributors to post-infarction damage. These perspectives postulate other relevant inflammatory mechanisms, such as neurohumoral imbalances, a weakened immune system, and genetic predispositions, which expand a more holistic view of post-infarction mechanisms.

Because myocardial infarctions and their associated complications affect millions of people worldwide, resolving these signaling pathways remains a critical priority. The authors emphasize that it is imperative to understand the inflammatory pathways disrupted by the neurocardiac axis and their functional outcomes.

Subject of Research: Neurocardiac axis dysregulation and inflammatory signaling following myocardial infarction

Article Title: The Neurocardiac Axis in Myocardial Infarction: Emerging Role of Brain-Heart Inflammatory Signaling

Article References: Kim, C. Y., Sakr, A., Bax, R., & Doycheva, D. (2026). The Neurocardiac Axis in Myocardial Infarction: Emerging Role of Brain-Heart Inflammatory Signaling. Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology, 46(1), Article 168. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10571-026-01803-w

item.title: Ultra Processed Foods: High Amounts Linked to Stroke, Obesity Risk - Healthline
item.description:
요약

  • - Recent studies suggest that higher intake of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be linked to increased risks of stroke, heart disease, cancer, obesity, diabetes, and cognitive decline.
  • - Research indicates that fructose in UPFs is processed differently from other sugars — it bypasses normal energy pathways and may contribute to liver fat buildup and metabolic syndrome.
  • Another large study in Family Medicine and Community Health found that people who consumed the most UPFs were at a higher risk of developing chronic diseases, such as diabetes, obesity, heart disease, and cancer.

본문

- Recent studies suggest that higher intake of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be linked to increased risks of stroke, heart disease, cancer, obesity, diabetes, and cognitive decline.

- Research indicates that fructose in UPFs is processed differently from other sugars — it bypasses normal energy pathways and may contribute to liver fat buildup and metabolic syndrome.

- You can reduce health risks by lowering UPF intake through simple food swaps, like choosing whole grains, lean proteins, and brightly colored fruits and vegetables over processed options.

High intakes of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have been linked to multiple adverse health outcomes, including an increased risk of stroke, heart disease, cancer, and obesity.

A recent study published in JAMA Open Network showed that a higher intake of UPFs may be linked to brain damage and could lead to an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline later in life.

Another large study in Family Medicine and Community Health found that people who consumed the most UPFs were at a higher risk of developing chronic diseases, such as diabetes, obesity, heart disease, and cancer.

An earlier review in Nature Metabolism also showed that fructose in UPFs may contribute to obesity and metabolic diseases.

Together, these studies add to research on the effects of eating high levels of UPFs on your health.

A recent study published in JAMA Network Open found that healthy adults who eat higher levels of UPFs may be more likely to experience damage to their brain that could increase the risk of stroke and future memory problems.

The cross-sectional study analyzed 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate participants’ brains and measured UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ diet. However, among those with the highest intake, these foods accounted for 45% of their daily intake, compared with 16% among those with the lowest intake.

When comparing the highest intake to the lowest, the researchers found that those in the higher group had 1.7% more body fat and had a higher risk of vascular brain injury (VBI).

The findings suggest that there may be a link between high UPF intake and brain changes that could increase the risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

item.title: The overlooked role of flu vaccination in heart attack recovery - News-Medical
item.description:
요약

본문

A nationwide Swedish study links flu vaccination during heart attack hospitalization to nearly half the hazard of death over the following year, yet reveals that most eligible unvaccinated patients were never offered this simple, guideline-recommended intervention.

Study: Influenza vaccination during hospitalization for myocardial infarction and 12-month all-cause mortality: a retrospective nationwide registry-based study. Image credit: Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com

Patients who received an influenza vaccine while hospitalized for myocardial infarction (MI) were less likely to die over the following year than comparable patients who had not received the vaccine earlier that flu season or during their hospital stay, according to a nationwide Swedish registry study published in The Lancet Regional Health – Europe.

How influenza vaccination became part of cardiac care

Several observational studies have identified influenza infection as a trigger for acute cardiovascular events. This has led to research interest in flu vaccination as a preventive strategy.

In the randomized, double-blind Influenza Vaccination After Myocardial Infarction (IAMI) trial, vaccination during hospitalization reduced the 12-month risk of a composite outcome comprising all-cause death, MI, or stent thrombosis, in patients with MI or high-risk stable coronary disease. The trial also showed clinically meaningful reductions in all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.

Together with earlier trials, these results led to a Class I, Level A recommendation for influenza vaccination in European and U.S. guidelines on acute coronary syndromes. Contemporary Australian and New Zealand guidelines also endorse it.

However, in view of the limited real-world evidence, the investigators set out to examine how influenza vaccination is delivered after MI and whether it is associated with better outcomes.

Tracking flu vaccination in routine heart attack care

The researchers used data from the cardiac intensive care component of SWEDEHEART, a national cardiac quality registry covering all Swedish hospitals providing acute MI care. They included patients with MI who were discharged alive between November 1 and March 1 during four influenza seasons from 2021 to 2025. Patients were excluded if their vaccination status was unknown or if they had already been vaccinated earlier that season. Only the first eligible admission was counted.

Of 12,711 eligible patients, only 6% received the vaccine in hospital, and 94% did not. Among those not vaccinated, 84.9% had not been offered the vaccine, only 1.5% had declined it, and 13.6% had another recorded reason for not being vaccinated.

Vaccinated patients were younger, more likely to be male, and more likely to have had ST-segment elevation MI and to have undergone percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), a procedure to reopen narrowed or blocked coronary arteries. Unvaccinated patients more often had hypertension, previous MI, or previous coronary procedures.
